blocks.text: NEW TESTAMENT
John the Baptist. The voice crying in the wilderness: he preached repentance, baptized in Jordan, and pointed to the one coming after him.
SCRIPTURE SAYS
“The prophet of the Highest” (Luke 1:76); in Jesus’ words, “a prophet … and more than a prophet” (Matthew 11:9)
ERA
New Testament AD 1–60
IN THE DAYS OF
Herod the Great · Tiberius · Pontius Pilate · Philip the tetrarch · Lysanias · Herod Antipas
BOOK
None bears the name
HOW THE WORD CAME
Luke 1 · Promised before his birth
THE CALL
Called, as four accounts tell it
“thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John.”
Luke 1:13 (KJV) →
HOW THE WORD KEPT COMING

From the textLuke tells the call in words like those that open the books of the old prophets: “the word of God came unto John”, as “the word of the LORD came” to Jeremiah and to Hosea. Luke 3:2 Jeremiah 1:2 Hosea 1:1
From the textMatthew and Mark tell no call; their accounts of John open with him already preaching in the wilderness. Matthew 3:1–2 Mark 1:4
Before his birth he was to be “filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother’s womb”; when Mary greeted Elisabeth, “the babe leaped in her womb”. Luke 1:15 Luke 1:41–44
He “was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel.” Luke 1:80

Matthew says he wore “raiment of camel’s hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins” and ate “locusts and wild honey”; Mark has “a girdle of a skin”. Jesus said John came “neither eating bread nor drinking wine”; before his birth the angel had said he would “drink neither wine nor strong drink”. Matthew 3:4 Mark 1:6 Luke 7:33 Luke 1:15

From the textKings describes Elijah as “an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins”. The Gospels do not draw this comparison with John’s girdle themselves. 2 Kings 1:8 Matthew 3:4

Scholars' viewEllicott’s commentary holds that the dress “was probably deliberately adopted by the Baptist as reviving the outward appearance of Elijah”; Jamieson, Fausset and Brown call the girdle “the prophetic dress of Elijah”. Matthew 3:4 [10][11]
He preached and baptized; people came out from Jerusalem, Judaea and the region round about Jordan “and were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.” Matthew 3:5–6 Mark 1:4–5
He had disciples: they “used to fast”, he taught them to pray, and some of them carried his question to Jesus. Mark 2:18 Luke 11:1 Matthew 11:2–3

The people held him to be a prophet: Herod “feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet”, and the chief priests feared the people, “for all hold John as a prophet.” Jesus said of him, “He was a burning and a shining light”. Matthew 14:5 Matthew 21:25–26 John 5:35
Beyond Jordan, where John had first baptized, many said: “John did no miracle: but all things that John spake of this man were true.” John 10:40–42

HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
Herod laid hold on John, bound him and put him in prison “for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife”. Matthew 14:3 Mark 6:17 Luke 3:19–20
Matthew and Mark tell that he was beheaded in the prison at Herod’s command, after Herod’s birthday oath to the daughter of Herodias (told on Herod Antipas’s page). Matthew 14:6–11 Mark 6:21–28
From the textLuke does not tell the death; he has Herod say, “John have I beheaded”. Luke 9:7–9
His disciples took up the body and buried it. Matthew adds that they “went and told Jesus”; Mark that they “laid it in a tomb”. Matthew 14:12 Mark 6:29
Hearing of Jesus, Herod said, “It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead.” Mark 6:14–16 Matthew 14:1–2
TRADITION SAYS
Of Paula’s visit to Samaria, which Herod had renamed Sebaste: “There lie the prophets Elisha and Obadiah and John the Baptist”.[5] Who says so: Jerome, Letter 108.13, AD 404

Under the emperor Julian, “At Sebaste … the coffin of John the Baptist was opened, his bones burnt, and the ashes scattered abroad.”[6] Who says so: Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History 3.3, 5th century, of events under Julian
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
Not Elijah in person, but the Elijah Malachi meant
Albert Barnes (1832–1851); John Gill (1746–1748); H. A. W. Meyer (English 1874–1875); A. Plummer (Cambridge Bible, 1880)

John denied being Elijah returned in person, the sense in which he was asked; he came “in the spirit and power of Elias” (Luke 1:17). Plummer: “Christ is there speaking figuratively … John is here speaking literally.” John 1:21 Matthew 11:14 Luke 1:17 [37][38][39][40]
Elijah himself is still to come, before the second coming
Hilary, Chrysostom, Augustine and Theophylact (as reported by Meyer, 1879); the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew

Matthew 17:11 (“Elias truly shall first come, and restore all things”) is read as a coming still future: the Pulpit Commentary holds that the second coming “shall be preceded by the appearance of Elijah in person”. Ellicott reports that the words have been taken so “by very many both in earlier and later times”, before weighing that reading against the next verse. Matthew 17:11–12 [19][20][18]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture names his parents’ home only as “a city of Juda” in the hill country (Luke 1:39).
Scripture does not say how old John was when the word of God came to him.
Luke calls Elisabeth Mary’s “cousin” (Luke 1:36); Scripture does not say more exactly how they were related.
Scripture records no miracle by John; the people beyond Jordan said, “John did no miracle” (John 10:41).
The Gospels do not name the prison where he was held and killed.
Scripture does not say where his disciples buried him.
